subject: Mathematics
topic: Number types, prime factors and systematic counting
scope: Both tiers: classification, place value, primes, factors and multiples. GCSE Higher only: the product rule for counting. Natural numbers here mean 1, 2, 3, …; follow a question if it explicitly includes zero. Original teaching and practice, not official exam questions. Tier labels describe intended specification scope, not predicted grades. Author-proposed coverage is recorded separately from independent review and publication approval.
prerequisites: Read whole numbers and a number line.
objectives: Classify numbers and explain overlaps between sets.
Use prime factors to find HCF and LCM.
List outcomes systematically and justify a product count.

notes.heading: Both tiers: number families and reciprocals
paragraphs: Integers include negative whole numbers, zero and positive whole numbers. Natural numbers are counting numbers under the convention stated in the scope. A rational number can be written a/b with integers a and b and b nonzero. Integers, terminating decimals and recurring decimals are rational. An irrational number cannot be written that way: √2 and π are examples. A square root is not automatically irrational: √49=7. A number can belong to several families; 9 is natural, integer, rational and square.

The reciprocal of a nonzero number x is 1/x because their product is 1. The reciprocal of 3/4 is 4/3, and that of −5 is −1/5. Zero has no reciprocal: no number multiplied by zero is 1. A square number has the form k² and a cube number k³ for an integer k. Some numbers, such as 64, are both.

notes.heading: Both tiers: place value and number words
paragraphs: Each position to the left is ten times the place to its right. In 6,040,007, the 6 means six million and the 4 means forty thousand; zero holds the unused positions. Read it as six million, forty thousand and seven. One billion is 1,000,000,000. Writing a number in groups of three digits helps distinguish thousands, millions and billions. For decimals, the positions immediately after the point are tenths, hundredths and thousandths; 0.037 has three hundredths and seven thousandths, not thirty-seven tenths.

notes.heading: Both tiers: primes, HCF and LCM
paragraphs: A prime is a positive integer greater than 1 with exactly two positive factors: 1 and itself. One is not prime; 2 is the only even prime. A factor divides exactly; a multiple is obtained by multiplying by an integer. Break a positive integer greater than 1 into primes, stopping only when every branch is prime. Unique prime factorisation means the same prime powers appear however the factor tree began.

For the highest common factor, take only shared primes with the smaller exponent. For the lowest common multiple, take every prime present with the larger exponent. With 60=2²×3×5 and 84=2²×3×7, HCF=12 and LCM=420. HCF answers largest equal grouping questions; LCM answers first common repeat questions. Check that an HCF divides both numbers and that an LCM is divisible by both.

notes.heading: GCSE: systematic lists; Higher: product rule
paragraphs: A systematic list fixes one choice while cycling through every second choice, then changes the first choice. This prevents omissions and double counting. If there are 3 possible starters and, for each starter, 4 possible mains, there are 3×4=12 meals. This product rule is GCSE Higher content. The number of choices at a stage must be correct: for a three-digit code using 1, 2, 3, 4 without repetition, the stages have 4, 3 and 2 choices, giving 24 codes. If a restriction depends on an earlier choice, split into cases rather than blindly multiplying the original totals.

workedExamples.prompt: Find the HCF and LCM of 72 and 90.
steps: Use the smaller shared powers for HCF: 2×3²=18.
Use the larger powers of all primes for LCM: 2³×3²×5=360. Check 360/72=5 and 360/90=4.

workedExamples.prompt: [GCSE Higher] How many two-letter codes use A, B, C, D if letters cannot repeat?
steps: Fix the first letter: A permits AB, AC, AD. Each of the four first letters permits three second letters.
Multiply 4×3=12; AB and BA are different ordered codes.

misconceptions.correction: 9 is odd but has the factor 3. Primality is about divisors, not parity alone.

misconceptions.claim: HCF and LCM use the same prime powers.
misconceptions.correction: Use smaller shared powers for HCF and larger powers across both numbers for LCM.

flashcards.front: When can you multiply choice counts?
flashcards.back: When each stage has the stated number of choices for every relevant earlier choice; otherwise split cases.

questions.prompt: [GCSE Foundation/Higher; IGCSE Core/Extended] Classify −8, 0.125, √81 and √7 as rational or irrational. Identify which are integers.
questions.answer: −8, 0.125 and √81 are rational; √7 is irrational. −8 and √81=9 are integers.
solution: √7 is not a square root of a perfect square; it is irrational.

questions.prompt: [GCSE Foundation/Higher; IGCSE Core/Extended] Write seven billion, two million and forty in digits. State the value of the digit 2.
solution: Separate billions, millions, thousands and units.

questions.prompt: [GCSE Foundation/Higher; IGCSE Core/Extended] Explain why 1 and 91 are not prime, and give the prime factors of 91.
questions.answer: 1 has only one positive factor; 91=7×13 is composite.
solution: A prime needs exactly two positive factors.

questions.prompt: [GCSE Foundation/Higher; IGCSE Core/Extended] Two alarms sound every 48 and 60 minutes. They sound together now. When do they next coincide? Also find the largest equal length into which 48 cm and 60 cm ribbons can both be cut without waste.
markingPoints: Use LCM for the alarms and obtain 240 minutes.
Use HCF for the ribbon and obtain 12 cm.

questions.prompt: [GCSE Foundation/Higher; IGCSE Core/Extended] Find the reciprocals of −2/7 and 0.4. Explain why the same operation is undefined for zero.
solution: Invert the nonzero fraction; write 0.4=2/5 before inverting.
Check each product is 1, then compare with multiplication by zero.

questions.prompt: [GCSE Foundation/Higher; IGCSE Core/Extended] Which of 36, 64 and 125 are squares, cubes or both? Give an integer base for each claim.
questions.answer: 36=6² is a square; 64=8²=4³ is both; 125=5³ is a cube.
solution: Compare with successive integer squares and cubes.
64 appears in both lists; 36 is not a cube and 125 is not a square.
markingPoints: Support each classification with the stated powers.

questions.prompt: [GCSE Foundation/Higher] A spinner shows 1, 2 or 3 and a coin shows H or T. List every ordered outcome systematically.
solution: Hold the spinner result fixed while listing both coin results.
Repeat for 1, 2 and 3 to give six outcomes with no duplicates.
markingPoints: Use an order which demonstrates no case is missing.

questions.prompt: [GCSE Higher] How many three-digit even numbers can be made from 1, 2, 3, 4 without repeating a digit?
solution: Choose the final digit: 2 or 4, giving 2 choices.
Choose the first from 3 remaining digits and the middle from 2; 2×3×2=12.

revisionGuide.summary: Separate number classification, divisibility and counting. A correct numerical result needs the right model: largest equal groups use HCF, first common repeats use LCM, and ordered choices need a systematic list or justified product.
keyIdeas: Is 1 prime? No; it has only one positive factor.
What makes a number rational? It can be expressed as a ratio of integers with nonzero denominator.
Can zero have a reciprocal? No; zero times any number is zero.
Which powers give the HCF? The smaller exponents of shared primes.
When can you multiply choice counts? When each stage has the stated number of choices for every relevant earlier choice; otherwise split cases.
